t019: Halo is an open-source AI assistant for Android. Ask by voice or text, use supported phone actions, keep notes and files in one workspace, and study from your own material. Run a model on your phone or connect a provider you choose. Glasses are optional; other host platforms are still in development.

t077: Ask Halo to do something on your phone.
t078: Halo has tools for timers, volume, opening apps and interacting with visible screen controls. Permissions and confirmations apply. Some multi-step actions and third-party app handoffs are still being tested.
t080: Set alarms and timers. Change volume, ringer mode, brightness and flashlight. Open settings and apps.
t081: Examples: “Set a timer for 12 minutes.” · “Put the phone on vibrate.”
t083: Find contacts, open the dialer, launch navigation, open URLs, search the web, share text and control media.
t084: When an action is handed to another app, Halo reports that the request was dispatched. Completion may still be unconfirmed.
t086: Inspect device, battery and network state; read clipboard text; fetch a web page; search files and Notebook.
t087: Access to sensitive data follows tool policies and approval rules.
t089: Read the current Android screen, find UI elements, and use accessibility-backed click, scroll and text entry when needed.
t090: Screen-changing accessibility actions are explicitly confirmation-gated.
t092: A request is not proof it worked.
t093: Halo records attempted actions and their outcomes. If another app takes over or Android cannot confirm the result, the assistant should report that rather than claim the task is finished.
t096: Install a supported model on the phone, connect to a computer on your network, or configure a cloud provider. Halo keeps the same tools and workspace; network-based models may receive the context needed for your request.
t098: LiteRT-LM provides on-device inference. Qwen 3 0.6B Dynamic INT4 is the current testing baseline; compatibility, speed and memory use depend on your phone.

t116: A clear workspace for your AI.
t117: Halo keeps your work in Notebook. You choose what enters the working context. Study turns selected material into a saved learning session, so your work can extend beyond chat history.
t123: Add or remove workspace items from Halo’s context so you can see what the assistant is using.
t126: Keep notes, files, conversations and collections together. Canvas gives you a visual space for ideas, images and documents. PDF tools are still in development.
t128: Study sessions bind to a source revision, persist attempts before AI feedback, track review history and can narrate through Halo's speech route.
t131: Notebook storage and cognitive memory are separate concepts. Promoting something into memory is a distinct action, not an automatic side effect of writing a note.
t133: Start with Android. Add devices later.
t134: You do not need glasses to use Halo. Android is the first host platform. Glasses, headsets and experimental robots can add input or output, but support varies by device and is still being tested.
t138: The Android app contains the assistant, model setup, phone tools, Notebook and Study. Some workflows still need validation on physical devices.
t141: HeyCyan glasses are the current Bluetooth and microphone integration target. Some speaker and media paths still need physical testing.
t144: Supported Android headsets can provide microphone and audio output, depending on routing and permissions.
t146: BuddyBot is a robot project exploring physical actions and safety. It is experimental and not needed to use Halo.
t148: Why Halo has a separate runtime.
t149: The runtime coordinates input, context, the selected AI model, permissions and tool execution. That separation is intended to support different models and future host platforms without rebuilding the assistant for every device.
t162: Connected devices report what they can do. Halo does not assume every device has the same sensors or controls.
t164: Choose when data leaves the phone.
t165: Use a local model or explicitly choose a network provider. Remote requests follow that provider's data handling terms.
t167: See what ran and what failed.
t168: Halo records tool calls and their results so interrupted work can be inspected and recovery does not blindly repeat completed actions.
t170: Halo is an alpha, not a finished assistant.
t171: The Android codebase includes the features described here, but not every workflow has passed hands-on testing. Check GitHub Releases for an installable build. Expect bugs, changes and unsupported devices.
t173: A local model has answered on a phone.
t174: A small Qwen model has produced local responses on an Android test device. HeyCyan microphone capture also has real-hardware evidence.
t177: The phone-action runtime has compile and unit-test evidence. That does not verify every action on a real phone.
t180: Newer provider changes, assistant-role integration, long-running actions and some device audio routes still need full device testing.
t183: The repository separates implemented code, test evidence and known gaps. You can inspect the progress rather than rely on website claims.

t242: Start a lesson using the science PDF. Ask which days the plants were watered and how much each received altogether. Expected: days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11;

t249: Learn rather than just receive answers
t251: Say “Give me one hint, not the answer.” Try an answer, request another explanation, then draft practice cards. They should not enter the review queue without your choice.
t254: Import or paste the sample note. Edit it, locate it again, and try sending content into Canvas if available. Check Activity for an accurate record of actions.
t257: Try voice in your language, reconnect a supported device, switch an app language, or recover from an unavailable model. Skip anything requiring hardware or credentials you don't have.
t258: A missing feature, unsupported file, failed provider or missing permission is useful test evidence. Record the actual outcome.
t260: Even a confusing button is worth reporting.
t261: Tell us which screen you were on, what you tried, what you expected and what actually happened. Include your Android and Halo versions if relevant. Never post API keys, personal files, identifiers, or unredacted private logs.
